procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated June 7, 1967 of the Calcutta High Court in Criminal Revision No. 1100 of 1965.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant instituted proceedings in the High Court at Calcutta for quashing the criminal proceedings. The High Court at Calcutta quashed the process issued under sections 424/34 of the Indian Penal Code against accused No. 2 on the ground of want of territorial jurisdiction but refused to quash the process under section 406 of the Indian Penal Code against the appellant.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave from the High Court's judgment and order. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court should exercise its inherent jurisdiction to quash criminal proceedings where the allegations in the complaint do not make out a case.

facts: A dispute arose between two partners of a firm.
After one partner (the respondent) sent a notice for dissolution, the other partner (the appellant) withdrew funds from the firm's bank account.
The respondent filed a criminal complaint against the appellant for criminal breach of trust under Section 406 of the Indian Penal Code.

The appellant asked the High Court to use its inherent jurisdiction to quash the criminal proceedings, arguing the allegations did not constitute a criminal offense, but the High Court rejected this request.
law: The High Court has the inherent jurisdiction to quash criminal proceedings if the allegations in the complaint do not make out a case.
For an act to be a criminal breach of trust under Section 406 IPC, it must be shown that the accused was entrusted with property or dominion over it in a special, fiduciary capacity.
A partner's failure to account for partnership funds does not automatically amount to criminal breach of trust; there must be a specific element of "special entrustment."
application: The appellant argued that as a partner, his withdrawal of funds was a civil dispute, not a criminal breach of trust, and therefore the proceedings should be quashed.
The Supreme Court noted that to accept this argument, it would have to be established that there was no "special entrustment" of the funds to the appellant.
The appellant denied that any property was specially entrusted to him or that he held it in a fiduciary capacity.
The Court concluded that whether such a special entrustment existed was a question of fact.

It was not possible or desirable for the Court to decide this factual issue at a preliminary stage, as it did not have all the facts, which could only be brought out through proper investigation and inquiry during a trial.
Expressing an opinion on the merits of this factual plea would be premature and could prejudice either party in the future.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal, holding that the High Court was correct not to quash the proceedings. The central question of whether there was a "special entrustment" of property—the key ingredient for a criminal breach of trust charge in this context—was a matter of fact that could not be decided without a full inquiry and investigation at trial.

issue.issue_text: Whether there can be an issue of process in disputes between partners for criminal breach of trust regarding partnership property.

facts: The appellant and respondent were partners in a firm.
After the respondent initiated dissolution of the partnership, the appellant withdrew funds from the firm's bank account.
The respondent filed a criminal complaint against the appellant for criminal breach of trust under Section 406 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
A Magistrate issued summons to the appellant, who then sought to have the criminal proceedings quashed by the High Court, but was unsuccessful.
The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that disputes between partners over partnership property cannot lead to a criminal charge of breach of trust.
law: The general principle is that a partner who fails to account for partnership funds is typically liable for a civil action for accounts, not for criminal breach of trust.

However, an exception exists. The offence of criminal breach of trust under Section 406 IPC can be established against a partner if it is shown that the person was entrusted with property in a special way or held it in a specific fiduciary capacity, beyond the general capacity as a partner.
application: The Court noted that to decide the issue, it would have to determine if the dispute was solely a partnership matter or if it involved a "special entrustment" of property to the appellant.
The appellant denied that there was any special entrustment or that he held the property in a fiduciary capacity.
The Supreme Court found that it could not rule on this denial. It stated that it was "neither possible nor desirable" to express an opinion on the merits of this claim.
It was not possible because the full facts were not before the Court and could only be determined through a proper investigation and enquiry by the trial court.
It was not desirable because any opinion from the Supreme Court at this stage would prejudice the case for either party in the lower court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not decide the issue on its merits. It concluded that the core question of whether there was a "special entrustment" of property was a factual matter that required investigation and evidence. Since the Court did not have the necessary facts, it declined to quash the proceedings and left the issue to be determined by the trial court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate had the territorial jurisdiction to issue process.

facts: The appellant argued that the Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate in Calcutta lacked territorial jurisdiction to issue a process against him because the alleged offense occurred outside that court's jurisdiction.

The Calcutta High Court had previously quashed the process against another accused (No. 2) on the grounds of a lack of territorial jurisdiction but had refused to do the same for the appellant on a different charge.
application: The Supreme Court examined the appellant's plea regarding the lack of territorial jurisdiction.
The Court concluded that it could not make a determination on this issue based on the materials available to it at that stage.
The judgment explicitly states, "The plea as to lack of territorial jurisdiction cannot also be decided on the materials nor can an opinion be expressed on that question."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not decide the issue of territorial jurisdiction. Instead, it dismissed the appeal and made it clear that all pleas and defenses, including the question of the court's territorial jurisdiction, were left open for the appellant to raise during the proceedings before the Magistrate.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court should exercise its inherent jurisdiction to quash criminal proceedings where the allegations in the complaint do not make out a case.
appellant_arguments: Relying on the decision in R. P. Kapur v. The State of Punjab, the appellant argued that the High Court should exercise its inherent jurisdiction to quash the criminal proceedings because the allegations in the complaint did not constitute a criminal offense.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's complaint alleged that the appellant had dishonestly withdrawn approximately Rs. 92,000 from the partnership's account and removed the books of accounts, which constitutes offenses under sections 406 (criminal breach of trust) and 424/34 (dishonest or fraudulent removal of property) of the Indian Penal Code. Therefore, the proceedings should not be quashed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there can be an issue of process in disputes between partners for criminal breach of trust regarding partnership property.
appellant_arguments: A partner cannot be charged with criminal breach of trust for partnership property, as it is a civil dispute.

Citing Velji Raghavji Patel v. State of Maharashtra, the appellant argued that a partner who utilizes partnership funds is only liable to render accounts to other partners, and a failure to do so does not amount to a criminal breach of trust.
The appellant denied that there was any special entrustment of property or that he was holding property in a fiduciary capacity.
respondent_arguments: By filing a complaint for criminal breach of trust, the respondent implicitly argued that a partner can be criminally liable, especially when there is dishonest intent and a potential special entrustment of property, which goes beyond a simple civil accounting dispute.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate had the territorial jurisdiction to issue process.
appellant_arguments: The Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate lacked jurisdiction to issue process because the alleged offense took place outside the territorial jurisdiction of that court.
respondent_arguments: By filing the complaint in the court of the Chief Presidency Magistrate, Calcutta, the respondent implicitly argued that the court possessed the necessary territorial jurisdiction to hear the case.

cases.case_name: R. P. Kapur v. The State of Punjab
cases.principle: The High Court has inherent jurisdiction to quash criminal proceedings where the allegations in the complaint do not make out a case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court cannot quash criminal proceedings at a preliminary stage when the pleas and defenses raised, such as the absence of special entrustment of property or a lack of territorial jurisdiction, are dependent on facts that require investigation and inquiry to be established.
obiter: A High Court can exercise its inherent jurisdiction to quash proceedings where the allegations in the complaint do not make out a case.

Where a partner realizes a sum in his capacity as a partner and utilizes it for the business of the partnership, he is only liable to render accounts to his partners, and his failure to do so would not amount to criminal breach of trust.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that it was neither possible nor desirable to express an opinion on the merits of the appellant's pleas, such as the absence of a special entrustment or the lack of territorial jurisdiction. These are factual questions that cannot be decided by a higher court without a proper investigation and enquiry at the trial level, as the facts are not yet in the court's possession.
legal_tests_applied: To establish criminal breach of trust under section 406, it must be shown that the person charged has been entrusted with property or with dominion over the property in a fiduciary capacity, and that the offense is in respect of property which has been specially entrusted to such a person.
The High Court can exercise its inherent jurisdiction to quash proceedings where the allegations in the complaint do not make out a case.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's arguments regarding the nature of the dispute (civil vs. criminal) and territorial jurisdiction could not be decided because the facts were not before the court and required investigation.

To invoke the principle that a partner cannot be charged for criminal breach of trust, it must be established that the dispute does not relate to any special entrustment of property, a factual determination the court could not make at this stage.
The plea as to lack of territorial jurisdiction could not be decided on the materials available to the court.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's complaint raised factual issues, such as the existence of a special entrustment, which necessitated a trial for proper investigation and enquiry, thereby preventing the proceedings from being quashed prematurely.
policy_considerations: It is not desirable for a higher court to express an opinion on the factual merits of a case before investigation, because doing so may prejudice or embarrass either party during the subsequent trial.
